opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's actually one of the most underrated reasons to train the big model. People look at a 405B and ask, "Who's going to run that in production?", and that's a fair question. But internally, the large model is a tool for improving everything else in the family.

The most direct way is post-training. When you do supervised fine-tuning and preference learning, the quality of your data is basically the ceiling. Human annotation is expensive and slow, and for many tasks, especially complex reasoning, coding, and long-context work, humans struggle to write ideal answers from scratch. They're much better at comparing and judging. So once you have a very strong model, you can use it to generate candidate responses, rewrite and improve data, filter out low-quality examples, and act as a judge or reward model. The smaller models then learn from data that's much better than what they could have bootstrapped on their own. That's a form of distillation, not necessarily logit-level, but distillation through data.

There's also a self-improvement loop. Each round, the best model you have generates and scores data for the next round. If your best model is the 405B, every model in the family benefits from that higher bar. If your best model is a 70B, you're stuck with a lower one.

And it helps as a scientific reference point. Training at that scale tells you how far you can push the recipe, what scales and what doesn't, and that informs decisions for the smaller sizes.

So I see the flagship model less as just a product and more as a teacher. A lot of the gains you see in the 8B and 70B come from having that teacher available. As the open-source community picks it up for synthetic data and distillation, the value spreads well beyond what we do internally.

r001.rationale: The response says the large model generates, improves, and filters training data that smaller models learn from, describing this as distillation through data.

fable-5.1.text:
The value is huge, and honestly it's one of the main reasons we trained the 405B at all. When you have a very large model, it becomes a teacher for everything below it. We used it for synthetic data generation, for rejection sampling, for distillation into the 8B and the 70B, and the quality jump you get on the small models from that is bigger than anything you'd get by just training them longer on the same web data.

Think about it this way. The small model's bottleneck isn't really compute anymore, it's the quality of the tokens it sees. A 405B model can produce data that is closer to the frontier of what's possible, especially on things like code, math, reasoning, multi-turn chat, where the web is noisy or sparse. Then you filter it, you verify it when you can, say with unit tests for code or checking final answers for math, and you push that into post-training for the smaller models. So the big model is kind of a compute converter. You spend compute once on the large model, and you amortize it across every smaller model you ship, and every future version too.

There's also a research reason. The large model tells you what's achievable. If the 405B can do something, you know the capability exists in the data and the recipe, and now the question for the 8B becomes how to compress it, not whether it's possible. That changes how you think about the small models. You stop treating them as weak versions and start treating them as distillation targets.

And one thing people underestimate, it also helps with evaluation. A strong model is a much better judge, better at ranking, better at preference data. So it improves the whole reward loop, not just the SFT data. So for me, the big model is not a separate product, it's infrastructure for the whole family.

r001.rationale: The response says the 405B generates synthetic data that is distilled and used in post-training the 8B and 70B, producing a major quality improvement. This conveys training smaller models on data generated by the larger model.

astra-6.text:
One of the main reasons to build larger models is actually to make the smaller models better. You have a stronger teacher. You can use it to generate synthetic data, to evaluate responses, and to distill some of its capabilities into a much smaller model.

So I don’t see it as a choice between investing in a very large model and investing in small, efficient models. They’re complementary. You push the frontier with the large model, and then you use that intelligence to improve models that are much cheaper to serve. The smaller model won’t recover everything the teacher can do, but it can get much better than it would have been without that teacher.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models can generate synthetic data and that their capabilities can be distilled into smaller models, but it does not clearly identify training on larger-model-generated annotations.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the big benefits is distillation. A larger model isn’t just a product on its own; it’s also a teacher for the smaller models. You can use it to generate better training data, to critique answers, and to help select higher-quality examples. So even if you’re ultimately deploying an 8-billion-parameter model, you can benefit from the investment in a much larger model.

Of course, the smaller model has a limited capacity, so it won’t absorb everything the teacher can do. But a stronger teacher lets us push that capacity further. That’s why I see the large and small models as complementary: improving the largest model gives us another way to improve the models that are cheaper and easier to run.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models can generate better training data for smaller models, but it does not clearly identify that the data consists of annotations generated by the larger models.
